tier_reason: First-party chart images (docs/pics/performance/{baseline,tls,tcp}/wrk-*.png) compare Orion with Envoy; the repo holds no benchmark scripts, wrk commands, Envoy or Orion configs, and no CPU model, Envoy version or build flags are given, so it falls short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: '2x-4x better throughput and latency than Envoy Proxy'. HTTP chart (docs/pics/performance/baseline/wrk-reqsec.png), requests/s orion-mr-st vs envoy: 2048 connections, 1 core 46,593 vs 12,819 (3.63x, derived from page data), 48 cores 1,881,522 vs 310,231 (6.06x, derived); 16384 connections, 1 core 38,573 vs 17,059 (2.26x, derived), 48 cores 1,410,611 vs 514,254 (2.74x, derived). HTTPS chart (tls/wrk-reqsec.png): 2048 connections, 1 core 30,398 vs 11,268 (2.7x, derived), 48 cores 1,478,634 vs 324,135 (4.56x, derived); 16384 connections, 1 core 26,354 vs 14,096 (1.87x, derived), 48 cores 738,429 vs 483,069 (1.53x, derived). The latency chart (baseline/wrk-latency.png, microseconds, percentile not stated, lower is better) does not support a 2x-4x latency win across the board: with 2048 connections Orion's latency is higher than Envoy's at 2, 8, 16, 24, 32 and 48 cores (e.g. 48 cores 251,325 vs 201,636; 16 cores 193,495 vs 85,659) and lower only at 1 core (280,347 vs 323,953), about equal at 4; with 16384 connections Orion is worse at 1, 2 and 4 cores (1,879,395 vs 1,789,400; 1,944,476 vs 1,769,852; 971,338 vs 633,244) and better at 8-48 cores (e.g. 270,335 vs 1,815,855 at 16 cores).
corrections.caveats: First-party; the numbers exist only as chart images, and the repo carries no benchmark scripts, wrk invocation, Envoy or Orion configuration (docs/performance holds only performance.md; tools/ has no bench files). The methodology lists 'Envoy, Ng-proxy, and Nginx' as compared proxies and scaling at 1-32 cores, but the charts show only Orion (series 'orion-mr-st', a runtime mode the page does not explain) and Envoy, at 1-48 cores. Envoy version, build and config, Orion build flags and the CPU model are not stated, so tier C. The README's 2x-4x is lower than the 6x seen in the 2048-connection HTTP chart at 48 cores and does not hold for latency: the latency chart is mixed (with 2048 connections Orion's latency is higher than Envoy's at 2 and 8-48 cores; with 16384 connections it is worse at 1-4 cores and better at 8-48 cores). The TCP (L4) chart shows Envoy at 53 and 47 req/s on 1-2 cores with 2048 connections and 0 req/s on 1-4 cores with 16384 connections, which points to a broken or saturated Envoy setup in this testbed and casts doubt on how Envoy was configured for the other charts.
corrections.why_faster: README credits Rust's zero-cost abstractions and memory safety; its architecture section describes a share-nothing design with one Tokio runtime pinned per CPU/thread, zero-copy Bytes buffers and rustls for TLS (Envoy uses BoringSSL). No profiling or mechanism analysis is given, and nothing isolates the language from the architecture.

notes: Chart labels match the record's HTTP numbers exactly; added TLS rows and the latency and L4 observations. Shortcomings to record: no published harness or configs, no CPU model or Envoy build, latency half of the 2x-4x claim contradicted at 2048 connections (Orion latency higher at most core counts), Envoy L4 rows near zero suggest a misconfigured baseline. Metadata checked: Apache-2.0, 39 stars, 22 forks, not a fork, last commit 2026-03-02 (active).

tier_reason: Benchmark code is public (bench/run.sh, bench/bench.sh, bench/lib.sh, bench/Dockerfile, bench/conf/nginx.conf, bench/workloads.txt) and the routez build flags are stated, but the hardware is 'Apple M-series Mac (10 cores)' under a Docker Desktop VM (no CPU model) and nginx is a distribution package with unstated compile flags, so not A; first-party, so C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: routez: zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dcpu=native (native+aes+sha2 on arm64) with Zig 0.17.0 inside an ubuntu:26.04 container (bench/lib.sh, bench/Dockerfile); nginx 1.30.5 is the nginx.org stable Ubuntu package and HAProxy 3.2 comes from the vbernat PPA, both on OpenSSL 3.5, with compile flags not stated. nginx config (bench/conf/nginx.conf) is tuned: reuseport, keepalive_requests 100000, open_file_cache, sendfile, TLS 1.3 pinned to AES-128-GCM and X25519.
corrections.caveats: The author's own table is mixed: 10 KB static file 308k vs nginx 312k (a tie); full RSA-2048 TLS handshakes 1.0k/s vs nginx 3.6k/s; HTTP/3 10 KB static file 94k/s vs 247k/s; gzip on the fly through the proxy 5.5k/s vs HAProxy 15k/s; a new connection per request 187k/s vs nginx 231k/s; p99 at a held rate proxied 4.30 ms vs HAProxy 1.79 ms; at the held 208k req/s fixed-response row HAProxy's p99 (3.2 ms) beats routez's 3.6 ms; a reload every 2 s under load fails 74 requests vs HAProxy 0. Rows come from different passes: the 10 KB static row reads 308k (tie) in the main table but '343k/s, 10% ahead' in the 'rows that have come off this list' table. The README itself says two runs of one build on a busy Mac differed by 90% and that a VM is not a benchmark machine; numbers are a median of 3 x 10 s runs on Docker Desktop on an unnamed Apple M-series Mac. routez is built with -Dcpu=native while nginx and HAProxy are generic distribution packages. The build needs a sibling checkout of endel/quic-zig (public, MIT). No LICENSE file in the repo (LICENSE returns 404, GitHub shows no license), so usability is reference. Harness strengths: a correctness gate checks byte-identical responses and identical TLS parameters before each row, servers are measured one at a time with rotated order and pinned cores, and nginx gets its best settings.

notes: All claimed numbers match README.md (fixed 627k vs 529k, proxy 262k vs 208k, TLS fixed 582k vs 324k, TLS 10 KB 208k vs 152k, TLS new connection 17k vs 13k, p99 3.6 vs 21.2 ms). Shortcomings to record: VM on a vague Apple M-series host, single first-party run set with a stated 90% run-to-run drift, native-tuned routez vs generic nginx package, many rows where routez loses, no license. Metadata checked: 6 stars, 0 forks, not a fork, last commit 2026-10-03 (active).

tier_reason: First-party README table and pic/benchmark.png compare statico with nginx's 'return'; no benchmark script, load generator, nginx configuration or CPU model is published, so C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release with per-runtime feature flags; Cargo.toml [profile.release] is opt-level 3, lto fat, codegen-units 1, panic abort, mimalloc as default allocator (profile added in the 2026-09-12 commit 'Optimize release build for performance', after the table was last updated on 2026-04-25 'Benchmarks updated.'). nginx build and flags not stated.
corrections.caveats: First-party; no CPU model, load generator (or whether it pipelines requests), nginx configuration or nginx build is published, so tier C. The table was last updated 2026-04-25, before the current release profile (2026-09-12) and the removal of the tokio-local runtime (2026-08-20). The README's key observations disagree with its own table: they list tokio-uring leading at 1.39M, monoio 1.36M and compio 1.27M at four threads, while the table gives monoio 1,436,420, compio 1,395,047 and tokio-uring 1,393,573, so the prose and table come from different runs. The io_uring runtimes write a response pre-encoded once per connection (src/response.rs build_response; any Date header frozen at connection start), while nginx builds its headers per request, so the io_uring rows do less work per response. statico is a benchmarking stub that returns one configured response, not a general web server. Actix-web (798,809) is slower than nginx (832,082) at four threads in the same table, and the README does not say whether nginx used tuned worker settings. src/monoio.rs builds a Vec with Vec::from_raw_parts pointing into the middle of another Vec's allocation (forgotten after the read), an unsound pattern.

notes: Numbers match the README table and chart (399,025/1,071,433 tokio and 656,517/1,436,420 monoio vs nginx 286,960/832,082; ratios 1.39x/1.29x and 2.29x/1.73x derived). Set same_algorithm false because the io_uring rows send a once-per-connection pre-encoded response while nginx builds headers per request; standard tokio statico uses Hyper per request. Shortcomings to record: no hardware, load generator or nginx config; prose vs table mismatch; numbers predate current release profile.
